title: Schools Teach Boundaries
author: Andrew Barron
summary: High school principal Andrew Barron explains why he banned smart glasses at his school and uses the decision to make a broader argument about what school rules are for. He describes the glasses as a tool that lets students record classmates and cheat on tests, and speculates that Meta tolerates the harm because it needs the data to compete in AI. Barron stresses that he rarely bans anything, tolerating fidget toys and oversized water bottles, which is why the balance of harm over utility mattered here. The heart of the piece is the claim that schools are among the few places teenagers must learn to coexist with others, and that rules, from keeping hands to oneself in kindergarten to walking with dignity at graduation, are primarily lessons in boundaries. Drawing on a taxonomy of classroom, pedagogical, and peer prosocial behaviors, he argues that parents matter more than schools here, but that schools must teach boundaries when parents cannot or will not.
points: Barron frames a smart-glasses ban not as a technology panic but as an ordinary exercise of the school's role in teaching students to respect other people's boundaries.
He sets a high bar for bans, tolerating NeeDohs, hacky sacks, and huge water bottles, and acts only when potential harm clearly outweighs honest utility.
School rules signal norms of polite, prosocial behavior that extend beyond the building, including into future workplaces.
Even if the ban changes few minds, enforcing it opened conversations in which he could argue for respectful use of technology.
quotes: I banned smart glasses at the high school where I am principal. The glasses, which can record video with the tap of a finger and play audio, including AI-generated responses to questions, had gone from novelty to nuisance at a speed remarkable even for a Meta product.
Smart glasses seem almost designed to make people uncomfortable, or perhaps in the long term, to desensitize us to being recorded at all times.
Other than the obvious or illegal, it is rare for me to ban items. I have been tolerant of NeeDohs and hacky sacks and comically large water bottles even as some schools disallowed them.

School is the place where they have to get along with others, figure out what annoys them, and respect their boundaries. Schools are places with rules, and many of those rules are made so that students can learn to peacefully coexist in a room with 30 other people, a life skill we want everyone to have.

When we teach kindergartners to keep hands to self, we teach our first lessons about personal boundaries, and when we teach high schoolers to walk with dignity down the graduation aisle, we teach them about respecting a public space.
The teaching alone is not enough. Parenting matters much more than schooling does in this regard, but if parents are unwilling or unable to teach boundaries, we definitely want schools doing it.
it has led to a number of conversations and emails where I have been able to make the case for erring on the side of being respectful when using technology. I count that as a win.
